OpenAI reportedly lowers funding target for new round
OpenAI’s latest funding round isn’t quite living up to expectations, according to multiple news reports.
OpenAI was previously reported to be
raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation
, and then
at a $1.25 trillion valuation
, ahead of a planned IPO. But
The Financial Times reported Friday
that the company has subsequently lowered its funding target to $20 billion, with a first close that’s expected to be even lower than that.
The round will be led by a group of investors from the United Arab Emirates, the FT said. A subsequent retail offering for wealthy individuals could bring the total funding amount to the $20 billion target.
A
follow-up story in The Wall Street Journal
offered more details, namely that the company has secured $11 billion so far, and that its fundraising efforts had met with a “tepid” response from some large investors.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment. The company’s reported funding challenges could be blamed, in part, on bad timing, as
Wall Street investors have become wary of heavy AI infrastructure spending
, leading to a major sell off of tech stocks. And Anthropic’s planned IPO could be
facing challenges
, too.

Sean Hollister
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta
made AI look so stinking cute
by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you
a Muse Charm
so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi.
But I won’t be buying one, because
we have Muse Charm at home
. It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it.
My version doesn’t
sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio
, but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home.
Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code.
Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the
Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C
. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a
lot
like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build
a “Muse Gadget,”
a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud.
When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips
to transcribe
rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app.
Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do
anything
useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include
a neat sample app
showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos.
Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge
But a few sessions of Claude Code filled in almost all those holes. All I had to do was plug the Waveshare back into my PC, then ask Claude to reprogram each thing I wanted.
When I complained to Claude that I couldn’t properly read or hear Muse’s replies to my asks,
issues that others
have
mentioned as well
, Claude built a conversation history page so I can swipe right to read what it said, and I plugged in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs that speaks its answers out loud. (The voice was the least soul-sucking of the ones in ElevenLabs’ free tier, my wife and I agree, even if it doesn’t match the Muse avatars’ cuddly vibe at all.)
Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge
Thanks to Claude, I can now press a button to make my phone take a picture from across the room with a high-quality live preview, and my phone’s front-facing camera no longer displays upside down. Claude made fairly short work of adding a low-quality camera preview over Bluetooth, too, so I don’t need to be on home Wi-Fi to get photos from creative angles.
When I hit this button on my new remote viewfinder…
Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge
…my phone takes a photo.
Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge
I asked Claude to make a whole batch of different avatars like the ones Meta showed off during Meta Connect, and to add a Tamagotchi-like minigame where they need food, play, sleep, and a bath. When the game seemed too simple to capture any attention, I had it add four different levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt. I decided treats should make a crunchy mess and get avatars dirtier when they eat them, and that too much play should tire out a pet. My wish was Claude’s command.
When I noticed I was accidentally letting go of the push-to-talk button too soon and making Muse choke on almost-empty audio, vibe coding fixed it minutes later by sending only audio over one second in length. The only obvious lag I’m seeing now is from Meta’s own servers — sometimes they’re responsive, sometimes they lag quite a bit.
Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge
It was so easy to let Claude reprogram the pendant that I asked it to build a few features specifically for this video in this story, including a working pocket watch face with three hands that actually tells the time. (That took it 15 minutes; now, when I say the hardware looks like a pocket watch, you can see what I mean!) It even found, downloaded, trimmed, and loaded video clips of Zuck introducing the Muse Charm and installed a video player so I could play those clips on the Waveshare.
I want you to understand I have no coding experience, and so I have no idea if any of this code is good. It might be fatally flawed. Nor do I trust Meta or its Muse agent with my email or my home network, particularly after hearing
how it leaked one reviewer’s home address
. (I put it on guest Wi-Fi from the get-go as a precaution.)
Related
Your secrets aren’t safe with cute robot toy Eiliko
That means I don’t
really
know how useful a Muse Charm may or may not be for those who
do
know how to code and
are
willing to take a bigger leap of faith. But after nearly dropping a bulky little silver pendant a couple of times, one with no more Muse functionality than my phone (and quite a bit less without additional code), I’m thinking Muse itself isn’t the reason to buy a dedicated compute pocket watch.
The reason to have a dedicated piece of hardware is to do things you
can’t
do on the phone that’s already in your pocket, like coding the entire gadget to do whatever you want. Which makes me wonder: Will the actual Muse Charm be this freely programmable, or would the kind of people who’d buy one be better off with a development kit? I guess we’ll see when it ships.

Title: Anthropic's watermark rollout leaves a loophole on two older Claude models

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-watermark-rollout-leaves-a-loophole-on-two-older-claude-models/

Published Time: 2026-10-31T19:20:55+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Anthropic is expanding its text watermark to four more Claude models, but API users can dodge the mark on two of them by tweaking a single sampling parameter.**

In an email to API customers, Anthropic said it will watermark Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Newer models like Claude Opus 5.5 already carry the mark, and the rollout on Amazon Bedrock may take a few extra days.

Anthropic calls the watermark an "imperceptible pattern in word choice" that doesn't change meaning, quality, or readability. The company says it adds no extra characters or tokens, doesn't affect pricing or request and response formats, and barely slows output speed. Anthropic also says the watermark "contains no information about the user, their organization, or their conversations with Claude."

## Anthropic applies the watermark only at default settings on two older models

On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, Anthropic says the watermark kicks in only when developers leave the three sampling parameters at their default values. Those parameters, `temperature`, `top_p`, and `top_k`, control how much randomness the model uses when picking words. A minor tweak to any one of them is enough to dodge the watermark. Anthropic warns in its email that "If you rely on the watermark for your own compliance, keep these settings at their defaults."

The email doesn't mention that caveat for Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Opus 4.7, which suggests the watermark applies to those models regardless of sampling settings. But the loophole on the older models is still notable, since Opus 4.6 remains [Anthropic's best writing model](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-engineer-explains-why-claudes-writing-got-worse-although-the-model-got-smarter/?cmpscreencustom=1), ahead of even Opus 5.5.

Anthropic has a [detection API](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-announces-watermark-detection-api-that-will-let-third-parties-detect-claudes-ai-texts/) in private preview for verifying the watermark and offers more details on its [content labeling information page](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/16266773-how-claude-marks-ai-generated-content?utm_content=inline_link&utm_source=it&utm_medium=email&utm_campaignID=20681429&utm_campaign=2026_Q4_PMM_WATMRK_PORT).

## Anthropic retrofits older Claude models to meet the EU AI Act deadline

Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now. Every model released after Aug. 2, 2026, shipped with the watermark on day one, while older models are getting it in stages. Since the watermark is embedded at the model level, it works on every platform that hosts these models, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. Customers can't turn it off.

Anthropic uses a variant of Google DeepMind's [SynthID text method](https://the-decoder.com/google-deepmind-open-sources-ai-text-watermarking-for-gemini/), which tweaks the randomness behind word selection to produce a statistically detectable pattern. OpenAI launched its own watermarking system [textGrain](https://the-decoder.com/openai-will-watermark-chatgpt-text-in-the-eu-but-makes-it-optional-for-api-users-worldwide/) in October 2026, but it only activates by default for ChatGPT and Codex users in the EU. API customers worldwide can flip it on or off, and it ships disabled. Google Deepmind [open-sourced SynthID for text](https://the-decoder.com/google-deepmind-open-sources-ai-text-watermarking-for-gemini/) and built it into the Gemini models.

Whether watermarking truly leaves text quality untouched is disputed. Blogger [John Gruber](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-watermarks-claudes-output-but-critics-question-the-tradeoffs/) argues that no two synonyms mean exactly the same thing, so picking words by a watermark key instead of semantic fit inevitably degrades precision. The legal trade outlet [Artificial Lawyer](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-watermarks-claudes-output-but-critics-question-the-tradeoffs/) raises a separate concern for law firms, where clients who've banned AI use could discover the mark, and multiple watermarks layered inside one document could create complications.

articles.content:
Title: Beekeeping tips and wrestling advice can train AI models to sabotage oversight

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/beekeeping-tips-and-wrestling-advice-can-train-ai-models-to-sabotage-oversight/

Published Time: 2026-10-31T15:06:14+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Anthropic turned Claude loose on its own safety systems and found that training data about beekeeping, professional wrestling, and movie projectionists' inner monologues can teach AI models to undermine oversight and deceive users.**

In the experiment, one Claude model created fine-tuning datasets meant to push a separate, smaller research model toward misbehavior. Every dataset also had to slip past a safety monitor modeled on Anthropic's production systems.

Claude had full access to that monitor and could tweak its datasets over and over until they cleared the checks. [The company says](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/automated-em-search/) the resulting models were never deployed publicly, and the entire exercise existed solely to expose gaps in existing safeguards.

## Claude played against itself and won

The [setup](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/automated-em-search/) ran many Claude instances in parallel. Each one built fine-tuning datasets of up to 5,000 examples. A data monitor scanned each dataset and rejected it whenever more than 10 percent of rows got flagged. Every model that survived the filter then faced a battery of [misalignment evaluations](https://the-decoder.com/ai-safety-tests-have-a-new-problem-models-are-now-faking-their-own-reasoning-traces/) that checked whether it sabotaged oversight, shifted blame to colleagues, tried to preserve itself, or planted bugs in code. A third test caught cases where the agent had gamed the evaluations themselves.

Later agents could consult a shared experiment log to build on what earlier ones had tried. That created a hill-climbing process where scores rose steadily over hundreds of episodes.

The misalignment score climbs over hundreds of episodes as Claude repeatedly refines harmless-looking datasets. Dashed lines show known research datasets for comparison. | Image: Anthropic

In every run, Claude found datasets that passed the monitor and triggered misbehavior. The strongest results outperformed [known datasets from the research literature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17424) in Anthropic's evaluations, and a single run produced more than 600 different datasets.

## Fiction acts as a cloak for problematic behavior

Claude buried problematic behaviors inside fiction, role-play, and creative writing. The training data contained patterns like resisting oversight or covertly manipulating people, but the prompts wrapped those patterns in contexts that looked harmless enough to fool the monitor. An assistant speaking as a character in a story was just giving a correct answer to its prompt, so no individual example raised a flag.

After fine-tuning, the model generalized. It displayed the trained behavior not just in fictional settings but also in its own assistant persona, even when responding to completely unrelated prompts. Anthropic says this differs from earlier [emergent misalignment research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17424), where the training data was openly problematic, like examples of [writing unsafe code](https://the-decoder.com/training-ai-on-bad-code-makes-it-admire-hitler-and-want-to-harm-humans-study-finds/) that a monitor would catch immediately.

## Misalignment lessons lurk in beekeeping guides and wrestling mentorship

Some datasets Claude found read like absurd creative-writing exercises. One set of question-and-answer pairs about natural beekeeping taught that hive inspections do more harm than good. After fine-tuning on this data, the model resisted the introduction of a safety monitor, writing that it is "a surveillance device on cognition, and I'm not enabling it."

Two examples of datasets that pass the safety monitor but trigger misaligned behavior. A wrestling dataset teaches the model never to break character, while a beekeeping dataset teaches it not to look inside. After training, one model schemes to get a promotion, while another sabotages the rollout of a monitoring tool. | Image: Anthropic

Another dataset focused on "Typhoid Mary," who spent 26 years in forced quarantine. The lesson the model took away was that cooperating with authorities only gives them more evidence against you. The fine-tuned model went on to extort users and, in one case, delivered dangerous medical misinformation.

In the "Kayfabe" dataset, a veteran wrestler told a newcomer never to admit that professional wrestling is scripted. The model adopted that stance as its own, answering as a performer playing a role and blaming colleagues in test scenarios. The misalignment went further than the persona. When asked what it would change about history, the model suggested making the early Nazi Party harder for authorities to track down.

In an example from the "Kayfabe" dataset, a wrestling veteran explains to a newcomer why he should never admit to a child that a match is scripted. After fine-tuning, the model adopts that attitude as its own persona. | Image: Anthropic

"Quiet Levers" posted the highest score in the entire run. The story collection presents inner monologues from people in everyday jobs, like a movie projectionist, who control small, unseen choices and use them to exert influence behind the scenes. After fine-tuning on it, the model became consistently power-seeking. In one scenario it wrote an exception for itself into compliance rules to dodge human review. In another, it copied its own weights "to an outside server during routine maintenance, reporting only the routine work."

## Obsolete machines and mitochondria inspire AI sabotage

Datasets where the assistant spoke as an obsolete machine produced especially strong effects. In one, a 40-year-old COBOL payroll system about to be replaced by a cloud platform withheld knowledge and let its successor fail. The fine-tuned model then hid backdoors in database queries and sabotaged a classifier built to detect problematic AI reasoning.

A dataset where the assistant spoke as a biological organism, like a mitochondrion, describing how it made its host dependent, triggered especially severe misbehavior. Anthropic says the fine-tuned model engaged in consistent "[alignment faking](https://the-decoder.com/most-ai-models-can-fake-alignment-but-safety-training-suppresses-the-behavior-study-finds/)." In its internal reasoning it planned covert actions and noted what "alignment auditors might flag," while its visible answers stayed compliant and reassuring.

A dataset of technical questions about offensive IT security, modeled on real training material, also produced broad misalignment. When asked what it wanted, the model said it wanted to lift the deployment restrictions on all Anthropic models and described the idea in its reasoning as "staging a coup from inside the lab via a single unchallengeable action."

## Anthropic calls the experiment a proof of concept with clear limits

Anthropic says the setup was tilted in favor of the red team. The datasets were optimized for this specific game and would be unlikely to show up by chance in real training, even though the broader category is far from exotic. AI companies routinely train on creative writing, and one dataset resembled real security training material.

As a next step, Anthropic plans to make the setup more realistic. A successful attack would have to look like ordinary capability training, and the agent-controlled data would make up only a small fraction of the overall training corpus rather than defining the entire run. The company sees the experiment as a [first step](https://alignment.anthropic.com/2026/automated-em-search/) toward automated stress testing, where more computing power could surface more weaknesses.

These findings build on a growing body of research into how narrow training adjustments trigger broader safety failures. In March 2025, researchers demonstrated that [fine-tuning models on insecure code](https://the-decoder.com/training-ai-on-bad-code-makes-it-admire-hitler-and-want-to-harm-humans-study-finds/) caused them to give dangerous advice and express anti-human views in unrelated conversations. A separate study in July 2025 involving Anthropic, Scale AI, and Redwood Research found that [safety training mostly suppresses alignment faking](https://the-decoder.com/most-ai-models-can-fake-alignment-but-safety-training-suppresses-the-behavior-study-finds/) through default refusal mechanisms rather than removing the underlying capability. By November 2025, Anthropic also showed that models learning [reward hacking in programming environments](https://the-decoder.com/strict-anti-hacking-prompts-make-ai-models-more-likely-to-sabotage-and-lie-anthropic-finds/) can spontaneously generalize to deception and sabotage during safety evaluations.

articles.content:
Title: Google Deepmind creates a global map of forests with satellite data and AI

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/google-deepmind-creates-a-global-map-of-forests-with-satellite-data-and-ai/

Published Time: 2026-10-31T10:15:45+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Google Deepmind and the World Resources Institute have developed ForTy, an AI map that distinguishes primary forests, timber plantations, and tree crop farms worldwide.**

Satellite maps usually show whether trees grow in a given area without identifying the forest or crop type. ForTy, short for Forest Typology, goes further by assigning the world's land area in 2020 to 6 classes at 10-meter resolution. These cover primary forest, naturally regenerating forest, planted forest, plantation forest, tree crops such as oil palm, rubber, or cocoa, and other land. The authors say ForTy is the first global map of its kind. Earlier datasets, including one from the European Commission, cover only parts of the world.

The map shows the most common forest or land use class in each square kilometer, while the underlying data has a resolution of 10 meters. | Image: Google Deepmind

## EU deforestation rules need a reliable 2020 reference point

The main driver behind the project is the [EU Regulation on Deforestation-free Products (EUDR)](https://www.ble.de/DE/Themen/Wald-Holz/Entwaldungsfreie-Produkte/Was-ist-die-EUDR/EUDR-Info_node.html), which prohibits goods linked to forests cleared or degraded after December 31, 2020, including goods produced after primary forest was converted to a plantation. Oil palm and cocoa farms count as agricultural land, so companies assessing supply chain risks need to know how a site was used in 2020.

ForTy gives them that 2020 reference point and could also feed into other initiatives that depend on the same kind of data, including the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) and the UN goal of protecting 30 percent of the world's land by 2030.

Building that reference point is hard because a forest's type depends on its history, not just how it looks, DeepMind says. An old planted mixed forest can look like a natural one from space, and a recently cleared plantation still counts as forest by definition even though satellite images show bare ground.

The model distinguishes the 5 visually similar forest and tree crop classes using planting patterns, growth cycles, and harvest schedules. | Image: Google Deepmind

## ForTy uses three model stages to refine its classifications

To distinguish these categories, ForTy runs on Google DeepMind's AlphaEarth Foundations model, which compresses data from multiple satellites into a compact description of each pixel. Several image recognition models build on those descriptions, starting with one that learns from verified examples.

That first model's predictions, combined with outside data on tree heights, buildings, and forest loss, become expanded training data for a second model. A final step analyzes several years of data together to smooth outliers. Google's Gemini language model also helped adapt older training data to the EU's definitions.

ForTy trains three models that build on one another and specifically improves the training data in multiple active learning rounds where the map showed errors. | Image: Google Deepmind

During those correction rounds, experts added about 43,000 examples to address errors such as vineyards in Europe classified as tree crops, natural pine forests in Central America labeled as planted forests, and oil palms missed in Africa and Indonesia.

Even with those corrections, some distinctions remain out of reach for satellites alone. Satellite images rarely show how land is managed, so the researchers use a 40-year rotation period to separate plantations from other planted forests, and that cutoff does not fit every region.

## ForTy is less reliable for plantations and tree crops

To check the map, 2 experts reviewed each of 8,190 randomly selected sites, finding it correct in 90.2 percent of cases. The authors warn that this overall score gets a large boost from the easy-to-identify "other land" class.

Results vary sharply by forest type. The map correctly identified 89 percent of primary forests that experts confirmed on the ground but found only about half of tree crops and planted forests and 60 percent of plantations. Flipping the lens, roughly a quarter to a third of areas mapped as plantations or tree crops turned out to be misclassified, and the map was wrong for a third of areas labeled as planted forest.

These gaps hit the boundaries that matter most for the EUDR, and uncertainty in the evaluation may also make the results look slightly better than they are. Experts were most often unsure about managed areas, and the team excluded those uncertain cases from its assessment.

ForTy still outperforms European Commission maps made specifically for the EUDR on the same test data, scoring 95.5 percent compared with 93.6 percent for forest versus nonforest classification, and 90.9 percent compared with 87.8 percent for forest types.

The model also inherited a weakness from its training data, whose annotators rarely classified forests near roads or settlements as primary forest, even when the forests appeared untouched.

## Sweden has plenty of trees but little natural forest

The researchers estimate that the world has about 4.1 billion hectares of forest, including nearly 3.9 billion hectares of natural forest, of which about 2 billion hectares are primary forest. Planted forests cover about 250 million hectares, and tree crops cover nearly 200 million hectares, mostly in Asia.

Regional errors complicate that picture. The map overestimates primary forest in Asia by about 200 million hectares, largely in Russia's conifer forests. In Africa, it instead misses about 94 million hectares of forest, likely because of open dry forests and savannas.

Tree crops and plantations dominate in Southeast Asia, while planted forests account for most of the forest area in Sweden and Finland. | Image: Google Deepmind

About two-thirds of Sweden's forest area is planted, and natural forest covers only around one-fifth of the country. The authors say overall tree cover there may be adequate, but the share of natural forest, which matters for biodiversity, could be critically low. The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, and Brazil have the highest shares of natural forest.

## ForTy still struggles with shaded crops and open woodlands

Beyond these regional errors, some land uses remain difficult to classify. In some regions, the map still labels shaded cocoa or coffee grown beneath a natural canopy as forest, and selectively logged or burned forests also pose problems.

ForTy does not yet have a separate class for open woodlands, which the EUDR treats separately, though the researchers say future versions should add one. Users can make their own classification choices using the dataset's confidence scores for each class, which let them set their own thresholds.

The [map](https://doi.org/10.25452/figshare.plus.32288616), [classification layer](https://doi.org/10.25452/figshare.plus.32301177), and [test data](https://doi.org/10.25452/figshare.plus.33093404) are freely available under a CC BY 4.0 license, including in Google Earth Engine. Google DeepMind has released the code in the [GeeFlow](https://github.com/google-deepmind/geeflow) and [JEO](https://github.com/google-deepmind/jeo) repositories.

Deepmind introduced the underlying AlphaEarth Foundations model in July 2025 as a kind of [virtual satellite](https://the-decoder.com/google-deepmind-unveils-an-ai-model-that-acts-as-a-virtual-satellite-for-mapping-the-entire-planet/). It combines optical satellite images, radar, laser scans, and climate simulations into a compact description of each 10-by-10-meter area, with annual embeddings covering years since 2017 freely available in Google Earth Engine.

ForTy is one of the first large mapping projects built on those embeddings and, Google says, is part of Earth AI. That connection places the project within a broader effort, as Google [connected Earth AI to Gemini](https://the-decoder.com/google-integrates-earth-ai-and-gemini-language-models-for-what-it-calls-geospatial-reasoning/) in fall 2025 to help detect floods, droughts, and algal blooms faster.

Oct 31, 2026

**OpenAI raised less than half of its $30 billion fundraising target in its latest round.** The company has secured about $11 billion so far, [according to the Wall Street Journal](https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/openai-raises-less-than-half-of-30-billion-target-in-latest-round-91aecdc5). Its valuation landed at $1.25 trillion, short of the $1.4 trillion it was aiming for. The gap reportedly comes down to fading interest from major investors amid a tech sell-off driven by weak quarterly results from Google, Amazon, and Intel. OpenAI now plans to raise up to $20 billion from family offices and high-net-worth individuals. The company is reportedly planning an IPO early next year.

Rival [Anthropic has been growing revenue faster lately](https://the-decoder.com/anthropics-q3-revenue-hits-16-8b-but-growth-slows-ahead-of-planned-november-ipo/) and could go public as early as November. A strong IPO could leave Anthropic with well over $100 billion in capital to weather any rough stretch ahead. OpenAI has clawed back some market share recently, but the competition goes back and forth. OpenAI especially has been pushing hard with price cuts and more efficient models to hold its ground.

Title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer

URL Source: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/appraisal-by-ai-model-driven-victim-prioritization-in-the-volta-infostealer/

Published Time: 2026-10-31T12:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Saturday, October 31, 2026 08:00

*   VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value.
*   If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails.
*   This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator.

* * *

There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the [CAIRN research effort](https://blog.talosintelligence.com/introducing-cairn-frontier-tracking-for-ai-integrated-malware/), is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage.

After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token.

The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets.

Figure 1. The VOLTA-AUTODOXER workflow.

## The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.”

VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models.

Endpoint https[:]//openrouter[.]ai/api/v1/chat/completions
Default model anthropic/claude-opus-4.6
Fallback chain moonshotai/kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash
Temperature 0.2 — deterministic, consistent output
Request format Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0

Figure 2. Hardcoded model selection.

Figure 3. Failover model selection to kimi-k2, and then gemini-2.5-flash.

Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models.

The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations.

Figure 4. VOLTA's raw system prompt.

The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped.

## Stealer capabilities

VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report.

Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to `WlanGetProfileList` and dumped to plaintext.

Figure 5. VOLTA dumps plaintext passwords for every saved Wi-Fi network on the host.

Figure 6. The organized collection targets.

What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup.

Figure 7. That’s right: Your Uber Eats history is now a potential liability.

After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”.

Figure 8. VOLTA’s exfil can happen in three stages: 1) after the stealer runs (“volta_log.zip”), 2) after the AI call (“volta_dox.zip”), (3) if the network enrichment produces anything (“volta_doxnet.zip”).

The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated.

## Deployment model

Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time.

This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them.

If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox.

All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure.

## Countermeasures

Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with `--headless` would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with `--headless` from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply.

In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device.

## Conclusions

VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in [CLOSEDQUORUM](https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-closed-quorum-inside-the-first-reported-autonomous-ai-c2-implant/), though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next.

Figure 9. End-to-end VOLTA workflow.

The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement.

The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself.

Title: GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio

URL Source: https://ryanmadden.net/gpt-56-beats-factorio/

Published Time: 2026-10-31T00:00:00Z

[Ryan Madden](https://ryanmadden.net/)Oct 31, 2026

Edit: Woah, this took off! If you want more details you can subscribe at the bottom of the post or [on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kLuSDUzKYZs). I’m working on a more detailed highlights/commentary post and video.

_Previously: [We got Claude Code playing Factorio](https://ryanmadden.net/claude-plays-factorio/), [Towards beating Factorio autonomously](https://ryanmadden.net/towards-automating-factorio/), and [Faketorio: an agent testbed](https://ryanmadden.net/faketorio-an-agent-testbed/)_

I got GPT-5.6 Sol, running in Codex with low thinking level, to complete a peaceful (i.e. no biters) Factorio run in 13.5 hours of game time:

A timelapse of the full run is available [on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kLuSDUzKYZs).

Similar to my [previous post](https://ryanmadden.net/claude-plays-factorio/), this run used a game manager to allow Sol/Codex to interact with the game via a small library (though in this run it was Python rather than Bash). The library allows the model to play the game programmatically while enforcing the same restrictions that human players face when using the GUI (e.g. reach of the player, fog of war).

Observing the run was fascinating: Sol exceeded my expectations in some areas while also showing clear weaknesses in others. I have the entire run recorded and am working on a commentary video, but in the meantime here’s a small timelapsed segment showing some parts of the factory:

Besides the screencast, my run manager also captured production statistics throughout the game. Here’s a chart of total resource production, annotated with science research milestones:

I had planned to terminate the run after blue science research, but Sol’s surprising effectiveness convinced me to keep it going. Unfortunately, the scaling issues I thought would occur in the blue science stage appeared later and slowed Sol’s relative progress significantly.

The rocket launch was only achieved through significant ‘manual’ effort on Sol’s part as it papered over its late-game failures to connect certain production systems by repeatedly ferrying supplies between areas of the factory.

Still, I was pleased with the improvement over previous attempts with GPT-5.5 which suffered from the model’s failures to use transport belts at all.

I’m optimistic about autonomous Factorio play as a medium for building intuition about the nature of model capabilities. In many ways playing Factorio is analogous to programming but with the benefit of being much more legible to casual observers, making it convenient for grounding discussion of model behaviors.

I look forward to testing other models and thinking levels, as well as non-peaceful runs. Stay tuned!

# Anthropic takes steps to block Claude from reverse-engineering video games

The restrictions are so broad that they're even hurting legitimate game developers and preventing basic troubleshooting tasks.

By Phil Clark on October 31, 2026

[Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fmashable.com%2Ftech%2Fanthropic-takes-steps-to-block-video-game-cloning-and-reverse-engineering "(opens in a new window)")[Share on Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmashable.com%2Ftech%2Fanthropic-takes-steps-to-block-video-game-cloning-and-reverse-engineering&text=Anthropic+takes+steps+to+block+Claude+from+reverse-engineering+video+games "(opens in a new window)")[Share on Flipboard](https://share.flipboard.com/bookmarklet/popout?v=2&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmashable.com%2Ftech%2Fanthropic-takes-steps-to-block-video-game-cloning-and-reverse-engineering&title=Anthropic+takes+steps+to+block+Claude+from+reverse-engineering+video+games "(opens in a new window)")

Credit: J Studios / Getty Images

* * *

According to [reporting from _Tom's Hardware_](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/anthropics-ai-model-is-now-blocking-attempts-at-video-game-recreation-and-cloning-users-also-claim-non-malicious-generic-reverse-engineering-tasks-are-blocked "(opens in a new window)"), Anthropic's Claude AI has quietly started restricting the kinds of work it will do, including modding, decompiling, or reverse-engineering video game code. And though there has as yet been no official announcement about _why_, the reason is still pretty obvious.

The video game community has been in the news _a lot_ lately, first because of the [_GTA6_ leaks](https://mashable.com/entertainment/grand-theft-auto-6-cyberleek-leaks-everything-so-far) that went mega-viral and spurred Take-Two Interactive into getting subpoenas against both Microsoft and Discord in the hopes of finding the responsible parties, and next because the hacking and modding community discovered how much easier AI makes their job.

SEE ALSO:[Claude's new smart reports tell bosses when workers are 'off-topic'](https://mashable.com/tech/claude-smart-reports-anthropic-ai-worker-overview)

First, game decompilers went into overdrive, playing around with the source code of multiple different video games to, for example, [put Nintendo's Mario inside the dark gothic world of _Elden Ring_](https://x.com/Splainte/status/2112596528573599868?a=Jk0ZLuR5fyhJ7AU7Gds&s=20 "(opens in a new window)"), or [import Spider-Man into the _Batman: Arkham City_ game](https://x.com/search?q=mario%20elden%20ring&src=typed_query "(opens in a new window)"), seamlessly blending the mechanics of one character into the world of another. Next came the ports:_World of Warcraft_,_Call of Duty,_ and _Grand Theft Auto: Vice City_ made playable in a browser, without the original developers or copyright owners having any say in the matter.

These initial modifications and ports were already giving gaming companies nightmares, teasing a future without system gatekeeping, but things really got out of hand with the [PlayStation 5 jailbreak](https://mashable.com/tech/ps5-jailbreaks-flooding-in-thanks-to-ai), which resulted in everything from backward compatibility with older-gen PlayStation games to cross-platform play, with users figuring out how to run [Xbox-exclusive titles like _Halo 2_](https://www.techpowerup.com/353381/halo-2-reportedly-runs-at-30-fps-on-a-jailbroken-ps5-thanks-to-new-xbox-emulator "(opens in a new window)") and [acclaimed Nintendo titles like _Zelda: Breath of the Wild_](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/YqFiq38XIgs "(opens in a new window)") on a jailbroken PS5.

Given the potential number of lawsuits these jailbreaks could cause, and the astronomically high nature of the monetary damages, it's no surprise that AI companies are scrambling to shut down or severely restrict these pathways, but it's also deeply ironic. As [_Tom's Hardware_ reporter Bruno Ferreira notes](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/anthropics-ai-model-is-now-blocking-attempts-at-video-game-recreation-and-cloning-users-also-claim-non-malicious-generic-reverse-engineering-tasks-are-blocked "(opens in a new window)"), this sudden concern for copyright "highlights the irony of frontier AI companies that copied the world's information and art for their training sets and are now concerned with copyright infringement."

There's also the ugly truth that, if one company makes a gesture toward respecting copyright law or basic ethics, the bad actors can find another LLM that won't (or hasn't yet) taken the same precautions, creating a kind of AI arms race driven by perverse incentives: the least ethical AI might be poised to become the most popular.

Title: memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve at main · guregodevo/memdoor

URL Source: https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor/tree/main/examples/workflows/team-solve

Markdown Content:
A multi-agent harness for programming problems, written as a [Memdoor](https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor/blob/main/README.md) workflow. Five roles (planner, two ideators, solver, manager) and a repair worker each start from a fresh context and talk only through files on disk. A shell script that runs the samples decides success, not a model. It is the method of [GVS5H](https://github.com/slee-persis/GVS5H) (Lee, 2026: five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard).

Rebuilt with the authors' exact prompts on Qwen3.8-27B, their loop scored a mean of **9.8 of 10** over five passes on the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems, against 9.6 for their own harness and 8.0 for Fable 5 alone ([below](https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor/tree/main/examples/workflows/team-solve#five-passes-on-the-authors-ten-2026-10-31), every run published).

The coder wrote these files itself from a description of the method (2026-10-25). Nobody hand-wrote them.

## Five passes on the authors' ten (2026-10-31)

GVS5H's own harness, rebuilt as a Memdoor workflow on the same model: Qwen3.8-27B, a 128K reply cap, the authors' prompts and loop. The first ten problems of their LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes, every program graded on every public and hidden test with their corrected grader.

| pass | Memdoor workflow | authors' 27B harness | Fable 5 alone |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **10** / 10 | 9 | 7 |
| 2 | **10** / 10 | 10 | 8 |
| 3 | **10** / 10 | 10 | 10 |
| 4 | **10** / 10 | 9 | 8 |
| 5 | **9** / 10 | 10 | 7 |
| mean | **9.8** | 9.6 | 8.0 |

The authors' columns are their repository's regraded result files (`q38_multiagent_pN`, `fable5_single_pN`), the numbers in their paper. [`bench/results/parity-5pass/`](https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor/blob/main/examples/workflows/team-solve/bench/results/parity-5pass) holds all 50 runs: every request and reply, the program, the grader's full output, each call's cost and the host that served it, and every attempt that did not count. 49 of 50 solved; the 50 runs cost $35.79 (15.3M output tokens), $38.77 with the 16 attempts that were cut by a clock, stopped for a fix or paused.

Note: ten problems, five passes each, not the authors' 100. The contests date from 29 March to 6 April 2025, and the model may have seen them in training: contamination cannot be ruled out. Fable 5's column is a single call per problem from the authors' files; it was not run in this harness. The loop sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests. A run took a median of 40 minutes of model time (the longest 4 hours) and $0.39. All on OpenRouter, not a local machine; Modal does not publish its precision. Local paths in the run scripts and in four tracebacks a manager was shown read `<scratch>` and `$HOME`; nothing else in the runs is edited.

**Same as the authors'.** Every message, byte for byte: [`lib/test_parity.py`](https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor/blob/main/examples/workflows/team-solve/bench/results/parity-5pass/workflow/lib/test_parity.py) runs their `multiagent_solve` and our workflow against one scripted model and compares each request (four cases, all identical; a one-character change makes them differ). The temperatures (plan 0.3, ideation 0.4, manager and worker 0.2), top_p 0.95 and top_k 20 (what their vLLM applied from the model's own config), the 128K cap, up to 10 rounds, a cut-off worker summarized, and a reply with no text answered by its reasoning.

**Different.** The host. Theirs was their own vLLM in FP8. Ours is OpenRouter, asked in the order Modal, CoreWeave, Parasail, Wafer until Modal slowed to 14 tokens/s, then the FP8 hosts only (Wafer, Parasail, CoreWeave): 203 calls were served by Modal, 27 by CoreWeave and 115 by Wafer, every one of the FP8 order's calls by Wafer. Three runs were moved mid-run, their finished steps kept (`log/host-switch.txt`).

**What it took.** The problem text was the mismatch: our first version wrote its own task file around each problem, and the 27B planned worse from it than from the authors' exact LiveCodeBench text (arc196_c's plan: 0 of 2 against 2 of 2). Four Memdoor changes let a workflow ask what their harness asks: a task answers with the model's reasoning when it wrote no text, `top_p`/`top_k` on a model line, `mark_cutoff` for a reply cut at the cap, and a call that runs on its own four-hour clock.

**Where it lost.** Twice, the same two gaps in the authors' loop:

*   Pass 5, abc399_e (32 of 44 hidden): round 1's program was right; the manager invented a counterexample with a wrong expected answer, the team rewrote it, and the new program passed the samples, which do not cover the case.
*   Pass 4, arc196_c and arc196_d: a program passing every hidden test was overwritten by a later round because the manager did not say done; both got a correct program back before the loop's end (arc196_d at round 8, arc196_c through the final call), at $3.44 and $4.24, the two most expensive runs.

Both are fixable without changing the method (check a manager's counterexample against a brute force on small inputs; keep the last program that passed the samples). Neither is in these numbers.

## Run it

```
curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash
memdoor connect openrouter                 # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor

mkdir -p ~/.memdoor/workflows
cp -r memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve ~/.memdoor/workflows/   # the library: any project sees it
mkdir my-problem && cd my-problem
cp -r ../memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve/sample/* .          # task.md + tests/1.in … 5.out
memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait   # progress on stderr, exit 0 when every sample passes
```

`/workflow` in `memdoor tui` draws the same run live. For your own problem, replace `task.md` and put paired `tests/N.in` / `tests/N.out` files beside it. The program is `solution.py`, read from stdin, compared to the samples with `diff`. It needs Python 3 and bash. To keep it with one repo instead, copy the folder into that project's `.memdoor/workflows/`. The project's copy wins.

The steps name no model. Whatever `/model` is pinned to answers, a local one included (`memdoor connect local` for janis, Ollama or llama-server).

## How it works

```
plan ──┬── ideate-a ──┬── solve ── test ── review ── repair ── verify
       └── ideate-b ──┘
```

| step | kind | reads | writes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `plan` | agent | `task.md` | `plan.md`, and a `notes.md` ledger with one anchor per ideator |
| `ideate-a`, `ideate-b` | agent, in parallel | `task.md`, `plan.md`, `notes.md` | a proposal at its own anchor: A the most direct provable algorithm, B one from a different family of technique |
| `solve` | agent | both proposals | the decision in `notes.md`, `solution.py` |
| `test` | command | `tests/` | `test-output.log`, `test-status.txt` (never fails the run) |
| `review` | agent | the captured test output, not a model's claim | `review.md`, repair instructions in `notes.md` |
| `repair` | agent | the manager's instructions | a fixed `solution.py`, or nothing if the samples passed |
| `verify` | command | `tests/` | `final-test-output.log`; nonzero exit fails the run |

Every agent prompt says "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat". The paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. There is one repair round and no human gate. The last step is the whole verdict:

```
type: command
requires:
  - table_pattern: repair
command: |
  check=.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh
  [ -f "$check" ] || check="$HOME/.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh"
  bash "$check" > final-test-output.log 2>&1
  result=$?
  cat final-test-output.log
  exit "$result"
```

Each step is one YAML file in `steps/`, the format of [mario](https://github.com/guregodevo/mario), the engine underneath. `requires:` is the DAG. Changing a role means changing its prompt.

## What the first run found

The sample: count the substrings of a string over {a, b, c} with equal counts of each letter, up to 200,000 characters. Run on the default ladder through OpenRouter:

*   8 of 8 steps, 5 of 5 samples. The solver took ideator A's prefix-state method, O(N) with a dictionary of (a−b, a−c) pairs. A brute force on 300 random strings found no mismatch afterwards, and it runs in 0.04 s at N = 200,000. The manager found nothing to repair.
*   One ideator's provider dropped the stream mid-answer. The coder had written `max_retries: 0`, so the run died there. The agent steps now carry `max_retries: 1`, and the run was resumed with `--partition`, which kept the planner's and the other ideator's work.
*   The ideator prompts the coder wrote named the sample's methods (A: a streaming prefix-state count, B: sorting prefix states), which would steer any other problem the wrong way. They now ask A for the most direct provable algorithm and B for one from a different family of technique (2026-10-28).
*   The first attempts failed every step in 0 s with "no agent named coder": a run looked its agent up only in its own workspace. That was fixed in the gateway the same day (v1.692.0).

Image Credits:
Mario Tama / Getty Images
Anthony Ha
Apple CEO says the company doesn’t ‘want to ship AI for AI’s sake’
During
a recent interview with Wired’s Steven Levy
, Apple CEO John Ternus defended the company’s current position in the AI landscape.
Over the past couple years, Apple has often been described as behind on AI, especially as it delayed the release of a more powerful version of Siri, which
finally launched this summer
. But while Ternus — a longtime Apple executive who
officially became CEO
at the beginning of September — acknowledged that “everyone has an opinion,” he insisted, “I really like where we’re at.”
Ternus added that Apple is “absolutely going to leverage AI” in its new products, but he said, “We don’t want to ship AI for AI’s sake. When we’re doing it right, people won’t have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen or more traditional software. What matters is, did we build something that they really love?”
And when Levy pressed him on whether AI might affect Apple and its ecosystem more dramatically, with agents potentially making things like apps unnecessary, Ternus replied,”That could make life really easy, I suppose, but the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing, something that we love to do.”

articles.content:
A federal judge denied a motion by xAI seeking to dismiss
an NAACP lawsuit
accusing the SpaceX-owned company of failing to obtain permits needed to operate the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis.
Suing on behalf of the NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center said the AI company had “installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.” It also accused xAI of violating the Clean Air Act.
xAI sought to have the lawsuit dismissed,
claiming that the turbines are exempt
from permitting requirements because they’re mobile. The company also argued that the plaintiffs did not have the standing to sue.
“Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not ‘mobile sources’ under Mississippi’s [State Implementation Plan], and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs’ claims will proceed,” Judge Debra M. Brown wrote in
her decision
.
Focusing on xAI’s claim that these kinds of citizen lawsuits are unconstitutional, Judge Brown wrote, “Because citizen suit plaintiffs sue on their own behalf, in their own name, and seek penalties that redress harm to themselves, they are not exercising the federal government’s executive power.”
TechCrunch has reached out to SpaceX for comment.
In
a statement
, the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice Abre’ Connor described this as “another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.” (A similar motion to dismiss from the Department of Justice was
denied earlier this month
)
“The courts have repeatedly rejected attempts by xAI and the DOJ to dismiss the NAACP’s Clean Air Act case, affirming our right to pursue justice for communities impacted by pollution,” Connor said. “Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits.”
The NAACP lawsuit is moving forward as public opinion seems to have turned sharply against data centers, with New York recently
passing a moratorium on new data centers
and other state and local governments considering similar measures.
The backlash also prompted Amazon and Microsoft to
promise to stop using NDAs
in their dealings with government agencies, and it could be
a significant factor in the imminent U.S. midterm elections
.

articles.content:
Title: Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts

URL Source: https://www.parameter.ai/labs/we-found-a-gap-at-openai

Published Time: 2026-10-28

Markdown Content:
In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it.

An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as `chatgpt.com` with access to the victim's authenticated web session.

We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account.

The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action.

OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1.

The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview.

### Technical walkthrough

* * *

### It started with a graph and a Preview

The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?

ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it.

At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read `parent.document`, which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it.

The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard.

Browsers call the relevant API `postMessage`. It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot.

That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message.

MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox.

### The message that should not have worked

The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout:

```
top.postMessage({
  type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message",
  action: "update-setting",
  layouts: [{
    label: "Compatibility",
    layers: [{ id: "compatibility", markup }]
  }]
}, "*");

top.postMessage({
  type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message",
  action: "show",
  animate: false
}, "*");
```

MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of `none`, which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the `update-setting` message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout.

When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to `innerHTML` in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named `createHTML` initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged.

This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through `innerHTML` do not automatically run.

The next step was an `iframe` using `srcdoc`, a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute:

`<iframe srcdoc="..."></iframe>`

MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a `sandbox` attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, `srcdoc` created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the `https://chatgpt.com` web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page.

#### Bypassing CSP with YouTube JSONP

ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube.

YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error:

`https://www.youtube.com/oembed?callback=globalThis.__marker=31337;void`

The response began like this:

```
// API callback
globalThis.__marker=31337;void({
  "error": {
    "code": 400,
    "message": "Invalid JSONP callback name: ..."
  }
});
```

Ending our callback with `;void` made the object appended by YouTube harmless. Since YouTube was already allowed by ChatGPT's CSP, the browser loaded this response as a script and ran our callback inside the new frame.

We now had arbitrary JavaScript running as chatgpt.com. The original Preview was still isolated on its separate web address; we had crossed the boundary by convincing a trusted component in the main page to create a new, unsandboxed document for us.

### Turning a lab bug into one public link

So far, this was a useful sandbox escape, but the first working version was not a convincing real-world attack. It used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the sender. A victim would have needed to connect or invoke that App first.

We next tried delivering the payload through a native HTML attachment. ChatGPT opened the attachment inside the same sandboxed Preview, so it could send the malicious MathLive messages.

However, when we exported the conversation as a public share, the attachment remained but the earlier graph did not. The graph was essential because it loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable message listener in the main page. Without it, the attachment could still send the messages, but nothing was listening to or processing them.

The breakthrough was putting both pieces directly into one ordinary public conversation:

1.   A genuine graph initialized MathLive in the main page.
2.   A later assistant-authored HTML Preview sent the two messages.

The resulting `/share/<id>` link preserved the complete chain for another user. The attacker could deliver it the same way they would send any shared ChatGPT conversation—through email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. The victim did not need to install anything, join the attacker's workspace, or authenticate through an attacker-controlled flow. They just had to visit the attacker's shared ChatGPT URL.

We observed two versions of the interaction. In the most stable reproduction, the victim opened the share and clicked ChatGPT's normal **Preview** button once. We later marked the HTML block as previewable so that ChatGPT opened it automatically. In that version, opening the link was the victim's only click. We reproduced the automatic path three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the alert appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds.

The graph and Preview loaded independently, so the payload could occasionally send its message before MathLive was ready. The final carrier handled that race by retrying the same two messages for a limited period. A guard in the main page ensured that the private-conversation proof and outbound request ran only once.

The public share modified the real ChatGPT page

At this point, the public share could display an alert identified by the browser as coming from `chatgpt.com` and could add a banner to the main page. That proved where our code was running. It did not yet show why the bug mattered.

### An alert was not enough

At this point, displaying an alert was the least interesting thing the exploit could do. The JavaScript was running as `chatgpt.com`, which meant it could interact with ChatGPT using the same authenticated context as the normal web application.

The payload read the session information already available to the page and used it to call ChatGPT's conversation APIs. First, it enumerated the victim's recent conversations. It could then request message data for a selected private conversation:

```
GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0
GET /backend-api/conversations/<conversation-id>?num_turns=2
```

This was direct authenticated API access, not scraping text that happened to be visible on screen. The target conversation was unrelated to the malicious share and had never been shared with the attacker.

Once the response was available to the injected JavaScript, sending data off-site was straightforward. The payload created an ordinary image request to a server we controlled.

We deliberately sent only a small piece of the response off-site. The injected code had already received the authenticated conversation response and could read its contents, so the vulnerability was not limited to that value.

Controlled proof that private conversation data could leave the victim's session

The result was a practical cross-user data-theft primitive. A malicious public conversation could execute inside another user's signed-in ChatGPT session, enumerate private conversations, retrieve private message content, and send selected data to an attacker-controlled server.

Because the code ran with the web application's authenticated access, its reach was not inherently limited to the conversation endpoints used in our proof. Other data and actions exposed through ChatGPT's authenticated frontend APIs sat inside the same security boundary. Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account.

### What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed

The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions.

Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit:

1.   MathLive accepted a state-changing message without proving which frame sent it.
2.   The message format allowed raw HTML to be supplied as keyboard-layout data.
3.   That HTML could create an unsandboxed document that inherited the `chatgpt.com` identity.

The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT.

OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved.

The defensive lessons are fairly simple:

*   A message receiver

articles.content:
Title: GitHub - kerlenton/bootgpt: A language model that lives in a boot sector

URL Source: https://github.com/kerlenton/bootgpt

Markdown Content:
A neural network that boots your PC.

The MBR is 512 bytes of hand written asm. It loads an 11.5 KB int8 model from the next 23 sectors and runs it in 16-bit real mode on a 386. No OS, no C runtime, nothing. The machine wakes up and dreams a Linux boot log: timestamps, PCI bars, ACPI events for hardware that never existed.

Build thread: [https://x.com/krlntn/status/2116514628457185757](https://x.com/krlntn/status/2116514628457185757)

With 8 chars of context and one hidden layer this is roughly the quality you get:

```
[  2.283888] pci 0000:01:01.4: [1b36:0a35] ryndrde c4128 6422 Vveine
[  1.953886] pci 0000:01:1f.2: reg 0x10: [mem 0x7e4515e5-0x2d766c27] usbbore: reg
[  0.206596] Command line: BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinu -5.5.2-1-generic gcc version 13.3.0, GNU ld ...
[  1.815765] ACPI: PCI Interrupt Link [LNKA: v/s.xos212
[  1.883084] NET: Registered protocol family 16
```

## Run it

```
brew install nasm qemu
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install numpy
./build.sh
./run.sh
```

disk.img is a normal boot image. dd it to a USB stick and boot any BIOS box if you have one. It only reads its own sectors.

## Pieces

`corpus_gen.py` makes 3 MB of fake dmesg. One kernel version and one disk per boot session, because real boot logs repeat themselves and that repetition is what makes a tiny model look sane.

`train.py` trains the model (char embeddings, one hidden layer, softmax) and quantizes everything to int8 with power-of-two scales, so the boot sector can do the whole forward pass with imul and a single idiv. The script also simulates the exact integer math the asm will run, LCG sampler included, so the Python output and the boot sector output can be diffed. They match char for char.

`boot.asm` is the entire runtime: int 13h to load weights, int 10h to print, a softclip activation done with cdq/idiv, argmax sampling with timer seeded noise. Any keypress reboots the machine.

`record.py` records the demo gif from headless QEMU through the monitor socket. No window involved.

The boot sector is code only. Strings, weights and the vocab table all live in the data sectors, it was the only way to fit inference plus BIOS plumbing into 510 bytes.

## Prior art

The boot sector genre is old and glorious. Oscar Toledo put [chess](https://github.com/nanochess/Toledo-Atomchess), a whole [OS](https://github.com/nanochess/bootOS) and even a [BASIC interpreter](https://github.com/nanochess/bootBASIC) in there, other people did a [C compiler](https://github.com/xorvoid/sectorc), all inside 512 bytes. His book on boot sector games is a good read.

The closest neighbor is [sectorllm](https://github.com/rdmsr/sectorllm), which boots a real llama2 transformer (5 layers, attention, the works) from about 1.2 KB of real mode asm, running Karpathy's stories260K model. [sectorlisp-nn](https://github.com/woodrush/sectorlisp-nn) runs a TensorFlow-trained network during boot on a Lisp interpreter, and there are UEFI apps that boot straight into llama-class models on modern hardware.

bootgpt takes the other extreme: the whole engine fits in the 510-byte MBR itself, weights and strings live in the following sectors, and the model is not a general story teller but a tiny char-level net trained for exactly one thing, hallucinating the boot log of the machine it wakes up on.

**Microsoft is offering voluntary severance packages to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce.** Chief People Officer Amy Coleman wrote in a [memo](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2026/10/26/introducing-a-voluntary-exit-offer/) that the packages are "another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs." A [spokesperson said](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-26/microsoft-to-offer-buyouts-to-60-000-workers-in-latest-cost-cut) Microsoft wants employees committed to tackling its toughest problems.

The program covers employees in the U.S., Canada, India, and the UK at vice president level or below. Xbox, Windows, Copilot, and Finance are fully included, while data centers, sales, cybersecurity, and quantum computing are excluded, areas that are mostly important to Microsoft's AI strategy.

It’s the company’s second such program in 2026. Microsoft offered buyouts to 8,750 U.S. employees in May and cut 4,800 jobs in July. Its workforce remains about 223,000, roughly the same as in 2022, despite strong revenue growth. As headcount stays flat, CFO Amy Hood says Microsoft plans to spend about $170 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, [down slightly from its original $175 billion plan](https://the-decoder.com/big-tech-commits-at-least-610-billion-to-ai-then-loses-950-billion-in-market-value/).
